primary_focus: Practice restating the problem and running a 10-second example check before writing code to prevent solving the wrong task.
thinking_and_logic: The final approach scans the array and collects indices where nums[i] equals target. That logic does not address the stated requirement (two numbers that add up to target), which explains the broad failures on basic pair, duplicates, negatives, and two-element cases.
code_assessment: Compared to the answer key’s optimal pattern (single-pass hash map checking the complement), your code is missing the complement-search step entirely. The canonical solution maintains a dictionary of seen values to index; for each current value x, it checks whether (target - x) has been seen and returns those two indices immediately. Your implementation instead returns any indices where an element equals target, which generally returns [] and cannot satisfy the 'exactly one valid answer exists' pair-sum guarantee.

next_steps.action: Re-solve Two Sum using the single-pass hash map (complement lookup) pattern.
next_steps.why: It is the canonical optimal approach (O(n) time, O(n) space) and directly matches the problem definition.
next_steps.how: Use a dict seen = {}. For each i,x in enumerate(nums): comp = target - x; if comp in seen: return [seen[comp], i]; else seen[x] = i.

next_steps.how: Write down: 'Need i!=j and nums[i]+nums[j]=target' and test on [2,7,11,15],9 before implementing.

next_steps.why: Pattern fluency prevents freezing and reduces time spent exploring incorrect directions.
next_steps.how: Practice: Two Sum with duplicates, negatives, large n; then move to 3Sum (sorting + two pointers) and 'subarray sum equals k' (prefix sum + hash map).
